comments.author: aigamedev-mod
comments.body:
Hey u/Appropriate_Air7307, this falls under Rule 4. Sharing your game is okay here, free or paid, but you need to talk about how it was developed using AI, so the community has something to discuss. This post doesn't have enough on that yet.

To keep it up, edit your post or reply to this comment within an hour with some details on your dev process, like:

- which AI tools you used, and what for
- how they fit into your workflow
- problems you hit and how you dealt with them

"Made with AI", a list of tools or a ChatGPT bullet list won't cut it. If nothing's added by then, this post may be removed.

If you think we got this wrong, [message the mods](https://www.reddit.com/message/compose?to=/r/aigamedev).

replies.author: Appropriate_Air7307
replies.body:
I’m making *The Kings Park Incident*, a first-person horror game in Godot set in an abandoned psychiatric hospital in 2001. I use OpenAI Codex to write and debug gameplay code, run tests, and script some of the low-poly asset work in Blender. I bring in sketches, reference photos, and asset packs, then play the builds and give feedback on what feels wrong.

The spider creature is a good example. I drew its silhouette and used Codex to help turn that into a rig that could crawl on walls and ceilings. In playtests it kept getting stuck turning sideways near stairs. 

Getting it unstuck was only half the problem: an early fix let it turn, but a frame-by-frame check showed a leg going through the wall, so we scrapped that version. The next pass checked the whole posed body, including the legs, as it backed out and turned. That cleared the specific corner we reproduced. I’m still testing how it holds up in longer playthroughs.

I’d be curious how others here test enemies with unusual bodies. A path can look fine in the navigation debugger and still be physically impossible for the creature to follow.
